⫸ Part A — Creating Data Frames.

Question #1

a. Create a vector:
```{r}

scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
scores

```

b. Sort the scores in ascending order and descending order. What is the output?
```{r}

# Ascending order
sort(scores)

# Descending order
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)

```

c. Print your sorted result from sort-ascending. Check whether the names (“Ana”, “Ben”, …) stayed attached to their correct values.
```{r}

sorted_scores <- sort(scores)
sorted_scores

```


d. Create another vectors:
```{r}

subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

subjects
incomplete

```

e. Sort subjects alphabetically using sort().
```{r}

sort(subjects)

```

f. Sort incomplete using sort(). Observe what happens to the NA values by default. Now sort it again using na.last = TRUE so the NAs appear at the end.
```{r}

# Default behavior (drops NA values)
sort(incomplete)

# Keeping NA values at the end
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)

```

Question #2:

When you sorted scores, did the names stay correctly attached to their original values?

    When sorting scores, the names stayed correctly attached to their original values.

Explain why this matters: if you were sorting exam scores to find the top performer, what would go wrong if the names did NOT follow their values?

    This matters because if names do not follow their corresponding values, the data becomes mixed up and inaccurate. If you were sorting exam scores to find the top performer and the names did not follow the scores, an incorrect student would be credited with the highest score while the actual top performer would receive the wrong rank.
    

Question #3:

By default, sort() silently removes NA values instead of showing them or throwing an error. Why might this default behavior be dangerous if you were reporting “the lowest score” in a dataset with missing data, without first checking for NA values?.

    By default, sort() removes NA values without warning. This default behavior is dangerous when reporting the lowest score because NA represents missing or unrecorded data. If a student's score is missing, simply removing it might cause you to overlook the fact that the dataset is incomplete, leading you to report a calculated minimum score that does not accurately represent the entire group.


Question #4:

Use order(scores) and print the result. Compare this output to the sort(scores) output. What is the difference?

```{r}

order(scores)
sort(scores)

```

    The difference is that sort(scores) gives the actual sorted score values (along with their names), whereas order(scores) gives the original position numbers (indices) of the values arranged from lowest to highest.


Use the result of order(scores) to index scores itself: # Compare this to sort(scores) – they should produce the same values. Do they have the same values? Explain briefly.

```{r}

scores[order(scores)]

```

    They have the exact same values because order(scores) returns the index positions needed to reorder the vector, and passing those indices back into scores[...] rearranges the original elements into sorted order.


Question #5:

Create a dataframe from these vectors:

name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio") 
score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74) 
section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")

What is the output?

(Your answer here)
```{r}

students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio"),
  score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74),
  section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
)
students

```

a. Reorder the ENTIRE students data frame by score using students[order(students$score), ] What is the output?

```{r}

students[order(students$score), ]

```

b. Reorder students by score in DESCENDING order.

```{r}

students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]

```


Question #6:

sort(scores) and scores[order(scores)] produce the same final values, but they work completely differently under the hood.

In your own words, explain what order(scores) actually returns (look at the raw numbers it gives you), and why that output is useless on its own unless you use it to index something.

    The order(scores) function actually returns a vector of index numbers representing the original row or element positions arranged in ascending order based on their values.

    This output is useless on its own because it only gives position numbers (like 5, 7, 1...) rather than actual student names or scores, so you must use it as an index inside brackets ([ ]) to rearrange a vector or data frame.


Question #7:

Explain why sort() alone could NOT have been used to reorder the whole students data frame by score (try to imagine running sort(students) and think about what “sorting a table” would even mean).

    The sort() function cannot be used to reorder an entire data frame because sort() is designed to operate on single vectors, not two-dimensional tables. If you tried to pass a full data frame into sort(), R would not know how to sort across multiple columns simultaneously without breaking the table structure.
    
Why is order() the correct tool whenever you need to keep multiple related columns lined up with each other?

    The order() function is the correct tool when you need to keep multiple related columns lined up because it provides the row index sequence based on one column, allowing you to reorder all rows of the table together so that the relationship between columns remains intact.
